chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, May everyone be free from misery, May no one ever be separated from their happiness, May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the Wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind Teacher, source of all good; O Bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O Bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just as the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara’s pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O Bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma’s root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara’s ocean; O So that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva’s ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common path, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy Teachers, O Bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
We can again just explore the power of regret. We can meditate as follows. Whatever harmful actions of body, speech, or mind have done under the influence of delusion towards the three precious jewels, my father and mother, my spiritual guide, and others — all the extremely unbearable evil actions committed by me, an evil person, polluted by many faults — I confess before the deliverers, the enlightened beings. But I might die before I purify all my negativities. So please protect me so that I may surely and swiftly be freed from them.

Since the untrustworthy lord of death will not wait while I purify my evils, regardless of whether I am sick or not, this momentary life is unreliable. I shall have to leave everything and depart alone. But through failing to understand this, I have committed many kinds of evil action with respect to my friends and others. And yet my friends will become nothing and others will also become nothing. Even I shall become nothing.

Likewise, everything will become nothing. Just like an experience in a dream, everything I now enjoy will become a mere recollection. For what has passed cannot be seen again.

Just to explore some of these points — in particular that we have definitely negative karma in our mind, and that if it does not get purified, it will definitely result in suffering. Therefore, we must purify this negative karma. Again, just really take in these verses from Shantideva and think: I definitely have negative karma on my mind, which will 100% result in suffering if it is not purified. Therefore, I have to purify my mind. I can even die at any moment. So I must purify now — and develop this determination, which is the mind of regret.

Just hold it single-pointedly, really having a wish to purify this negative karma. Just really try to hold this determination to purify deep in the heart.

Then we can check in on our meditation break practice this last week. Just in the presence of our spiritual guide, ask: how did my practice go? Was I able to remember? In what situations did I happen to forget? And why was that? Just investigate like this for a few minutes. We can come to some conclusion about our own meditation break practice. And then in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

shantiDevaReading.text:
[37–38] In the brief span of this one life many friends and foes have already passed away and will be seen no more. However, the unbearable evil fruit that has grown from the non-virtuous actions that I have committed on behalf of these friends and foes now stares me full in the face.

[39] Day and night, moment by moment, whether I am in motion or at rest, my life is continuously slipping away and never increasing in duration. Since this is the nature of my situation, why should I not die?

[40–42] With my non-virtues still undeclared and the extent of my accumulated merit too small for me to rely upon, and with the messengers of the Lord of Death standing before me, how will I be able to lie on my death-bed without fear and anxiety?

[43–44] Seized by the authorities and led away to a place of execution, a condemned man will suffer a dry mouth, sunken eyes, and many other transformations of body and mind. If this is so, how much greater will be my fear and suffering when I am stricken by the great panic caused by seeing the terrifying physical apparitions of the messengers of the Lord of Death?

[45–46] Merely seeing the henchmen of the Lord of Death will cause me such fear and despair that I shall be desperate to find a refuge for my protection. With wide, bulging eyes I shall look in the four directions for someone who can provide me with safe refuge. But when I find no refuge I shall fall into utter despair.

[47–48] Therefore, from this very day I go for refuge to all the Buddhas, those who protect all sentient beings from fear. I go for refuge to the Dharma Jewel that is possessed by these Buddhas. I go for refuge to the assembly of Superior Bodhisattvas.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.text:
I've been working on purifying holding wrong views. I remember reading somewhere, I think it was this week in Mirror of Dharma, that poor concentration comes from holding wrong views. And my concentration's been terrible — it's been terrible for years. So I thought a lot about wrong views that I held in the past, and I'm really convinced that not only did I hold wrong views, but I taught other people wrong views. I really convinced them and was excited when they held the same wrong views that I did. So I've been purifying that.

I'm proud to say that in the meditation break, I did do better than totally non-existent. What I was thinking about in the break was noticing when I was holding wrong views, thinking about possibly what the correct view would have been, but also trying to recognize when I'm holding a correct view and rejoicing in it — so that I can build up some of the positive karma for holding correct views, besides purifying the wrong views that I've held.

The other thing karma-related that I've been thinking about and meditating on is that I have a tendency to procrastinate — oh, I'll do that later. And that just shows me that I really don't think I'm going to die right now. So I've been thinking a lot about: if I died right now, what would be left undone? And after I went through my list of worldly things that I really need to get done, the purity of my mind is the big one that would be left undone.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text: That's great. So investigating wrong views, correct views, and also just that habit of procrastination and using that as a little mirror, especially thinking about death, to motivate oneself to get a move on. Thanks, Fran.

dataShares.speaker: Suzanne
dataShares.text:
I think I need to do Fran's practice with concentration. But I've been doing the purification, and I said in the chat that I always felt I didn't really need to purify because of all the suffering with my chronic illness. And then I said, as an experiment, let me just try. What's going to happen if I do purify? So I did, and a lot of stuff was happening. I had a couple of fires. I burnt myself with the oven. That stuff seems to be clearing up now, and it seems to be steady. Nothing crazy has happened. So maybe it's like settling down. But apparently I did need to purify. So that was a crazy thought on my part.

The other thing I wanted to mention was yesterday I had my sister and a very close friend, a childhood friend, come over. And the friend is going through — she just finished chemo. She's going to have surgery in two weeks. She really didn't look good. She was very weak. It was very upsetting. When I was at the temple, I bought two little Taras, the mini ones, because I just think they're cute. I was going to give one to my sister and keep one, but I'm thinking, Danielle really needs this more than I do. So I wrote out the mantras and I put them in both little boxes and I gave them to them. My sister was thrilled because she's seen Tara help her countless times, even though she's not a Buddhist or anything. And Danielle was happy — she thought it was really pretty and cute. It was just really nice. I was excited to give it to them. So the mind of giving can be very nice sometimes.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, it's nice. Good Six Perfections Day activity of practicing giving — giving Buddhist statues to people. Thanks, Suzanne.

Regarding the point about purification — just even if we have some chronic problems or pain or a lot of difficulty, it doesn't mean that we shouldn't overtly do a purification practice. Those are two different things. We still need to do a purification practice.

Also, part of it is that when we're encountering a lot of pain or difficulty, we can purify it then by happily accepting it, regarding it as arising from our past negative karma. So if we're very vigilantly doing that — basically deeply, happily accepting — then it is a very powerful purification practice. But just experiencing a bunch of suffering and pain is not. That doesn't have anything to do with purification. That's just experiencing suffering and pain.

Sometimes people will say colloquially, 'Oh, I'm purifying a lot' — a.k.a., I'm suffering a lot. No, completely wrong. That's not correct at all. It's okay to say it colloquially, but it's not actually a correct statement. Because we have to be happily accepting, thinking, 'I'm regarding this as purifying my negative karma.' Then, yeah, fine, I'm purifying. But just suffering has nothing to do with purifying. We might actually be making the karma worse, because we could be suffering with a lot of anger and then just making it even worse and creating even more negative karma.

Just by suffering doesn't make us a Buddha. Suffering and transforming it to the spiritual path makes us into a Buddha. But suffering alone won't.

dataShares.speaker: Sumit
dataShares.text:
So somebody appeared in my life and they were problematic, and I was developing all sorts of negative views towards them. And then it kind of occurred to me that this person was just like this other person from my past. And it was great, because I just felt like this is my chance to purify my problematic — I mean, if I'm honest, I haven't left the point of view that they're problematic, but I didn't react towards that person with compassion before, for sure.

And it was just like, oh my God, this person is appearing to me as my opportunity to purify the way I treated the person in the past. It was just so amazing. It felt like this person is a gift from the Buddhas. It's so transformative when you have this mind of purification. When that's on your practice repertoire, these bad things — it really does feel like a gift to me. I guess it says that in the books all the time, but it's rare that I actually really felt that. So it was really wonderful to just feel that experience.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, thanks, Sumit. It's a really nice insight. These kind of moments are fantastic. You're right — it's showing the benefit of Dharma.

Having bad, annoying things happen to us without Dharma is very complicated to deal with. It just makes life terrible. And this is an example where with Dharma, you can just be like, woo! This is this karmic pattern that I keep avoiding, and I've avoided over and over again. I keep trying to run from it, and it's back again, and this is my time — I'm going to get it this time. And with that mind, we're not really that bothered in the same way.

It's really important to actually notice these kind of patterns. Certain kinds of people and things that really rile us up — they often repeat in different bodies over and over again until we get the message. It just keeps coming until we get the message. And then when we get the message, it just goes away. It's a very weird thing. They just disappear, or the people that are like them. And then other people show up that test our other karmic issues.

dataShares.speaker: David
dataShares.text:
So I spent this past week with my in-laws. It's like an annual tradition, and it's nice because it's a nice little Petri dish — I spend one week with the same people every year.

A couple things. One is I noticed it was actually a little bit difficult to practice, just being away from the center, having my routine a little bit disrupted. I did try to remember purification and basically regard any virtuous action as purifying, and trying to purify principally my irritation and annoyance. So if I make offerings, I'm like, let that purify.

The practice itself was sort of okay. But I noticed that in general, the whole experience — these people I spent time with, I've prayed for them hundreds and hundreds of times, and they're way more harmonious and delightful than ever before. So I really tried to just take solace in that — that sometimes it just takes time for these things to take effect.

I think sometimes with purification, my mind is very interested in real quick fixes. Purification maybe can be like that sometimes. But I think it's also very much about the long game. I've only known these people since I was still — just seeing over a period of time an improvement. Tried to really use that as fodder for continuing to practice without any expectation of results.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, thanks, David. It's fantastic. You're right, it does take some time with certain situations, and it's nice to use these kind of people who are regular occurrences in our life as a touchstone kind of point, or like a little mirror for our practice. Seeing them every year, it's like, okay, where is it at now?

Thanks for also showing that example of praying for them. That's the thing that really can help these people, but it does take some vigorous prayers and lots and lots of them over a long period of time.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 362–363: Wrong views — re-covering from previous class with new elaboration
teaching.text:
Page 90. Non-virtuous actions such as theft, divisive speech, and malice are committed with other beings serving as their intended objects or victims. There are certain mental actions, however, which are not directed outwardly, but instead affect the perpetrator directly. Such mental actions fall into the group known as holding wrong or perverted views and constitute the heaviest and most damaging of all unskillful actions.

With respect to holding wrong views, we have made this point clear before, but I want to make it clear again. The actual action of holding wrong views has to be a complete action. It doesn't just mean being ignorant. Just being ignorant isn't the action of holding wrong views. These are two very different things. We are all ignorant.

If ignorance was the same as holding wrong views, there is no way that we could actually leave samsara, because we would be creating the most heinous and negative action over and over again until the end of time. Actually, ignorance itself doesn't create negativity. It just means not knowing. It's what we then do that creates the negativity.

Holding wrong views and the complete action of it is actively denying Dharma, very purposefully. It doesn't mean just not acting in accordance with it. Those are two different things. Due to our delusions and limitations, sometimes we don't act accordingly. We are trying, but we are human.

Once we become a Buddhist, it's a little bit hard to fully create this action again. Even if we have doubts, we are usually not firmly against Buddhist truths. If we were, we probably wouldn't come to TTP. It would just be kind of a weird thing to do.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Wrong views ripening as difficulty in practice
teaching.text:
Related to that is that we have held these views billions and billions of times in the past. This negative karma basically ripens in an incredibly annoying way, which is that we are uninterested in Dharma. We don't understand Dharma. It feels confusing, frustrating. Or we just get no spiritual experience when we do it. That's really hard.

Some people don't make it through that into a hearty, vibrant practice. They practice. They come to a class. It's just gobbledygook. It doesn't make any sense. It's hard to wade through that. Or they meditate over and over and over again, and nothing happens.

Every time meditation does not go according to plan, it's so helpful to remember that this is probably one of the root causes. And it's nice to kind of frame it that way. It gets us out of low self-esteem kind of thinking — I'm bad at this, I'm not good at this. It's just karma from holding wrong views ripening. And all that should do is just motivate us to purify more.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
This shows the importance of just being also incredibly kind to people and creating an incredibly kind, welcoming environment where people set a very good, pure, spiritual example. Not just a group of friends, but we're setting a pure spiritual example and being incredibly kind to people.

Because that actually can help them wade through that period of negative karma ripening. It's like: okay, I don't get anything. I can't make sense of the teaching. I don't know how to meditate. Meditating is painful and frustrating. But these people are really kind and they are setting a really good example. And that sometimes is actually enough for someone to keep their head in the game a little bit longer.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 364–365: Purifying as prerequisite; four factors of non-virtue
teaching.text:
All non-virtuous actions, whether directed inwardly or outwardly, contaminate our mind. Thus if we wish to develop realizations concerning any aspect of Dharma, it's necessary to purify our non-virtue as much as possible. Before a dirty pot can be used as a container for a delicious drink, it must be thoroughly cleansed. Otherwise the beverage will be defiled and unfit for consumption.

To use a different image, if we do not rid our mind of its own defilements, the sun-like bodhichitta will be unable to dawn within it. On the other hand, if we do manage to purify our non-virtue and accumulate great wealth of merit, it is possible to gain deep realizations of even such a difficult topic as the profound view of ultimate reality without having to receive extensive Dharma teachings.

At this point it might be helpful to talk about the varying degrees of non-virtue. Some people think that the non-virtue of killing a small insect is insignificant when compared with that of killing a large animal. However, the mere size of the victim is not necessarily the most important criterion determining the gravity of our actions.

The difference between great and small non-virtue is determined by the interrelationship of four factors: object, time, action, and mind. The heaviest non-virtuous karma will be incurred if the object of our non-virtuous action is venerable and worthy of respect. In terms of time, the heaviness of non-virtuous actions increases if they're committed on days set aside for religious and spiritual observance or the taking of vows. The way the non-virtuous action is performed also affects its heaviness. Finally, the state of mind we are in when we perform a negative action greatly determines how heavy the result of that action will be.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Practical application of the four factors
teaching.text: I wonder if someone could say what do you think is the practical application of these four? It's not trying to get us to become karma mathematicians. What's the practical benefit of understanding these four? Let's say you're teaching this in a general program class — modern Brooklyn people coming, and you want to leave them with something they can bring into their life and make their life better today.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: Seems like mindfulness would be a big aspect of it. Especially the second one — on days set aside for religious or spiritual observance, it's good to be extra careful. That would be really helpful with cultivating mindfulness. Also just the first one, cultivating an attitude of respect and getting in touch with what does that mean? Could we adopt that attitude towards everyone?

teaching.speaker: Kristin
teaching.text: I was thinking that it is meant to encourage us — it might get a little bit overwhelming at the idea that killing an insect is creating negative karma, which it is, but helpful to know that if you were to accidentally step on an insect and kill it, that would not be as bad as pulling its legs apart and wings off. So I think it might be just encouraging us, like David said, to be more mindful and to try to pay particular attention to those first two categories, but also to just kind of know that these factors matter and our state of mind is really a big part of it.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: What came to my mind was just intention — that if you hurt somebody without an intention to hurt them, it's not a completed action. It has to start with that negative intention.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Summary of four factors discussion; animals are people; intention is key
teaching.text:
Yeah. And then Sumit, same thing. So that's really where we would want to go with this, especially if you're teaching on a GP. Making the point about the small insect and the large animal is helpful. Does size make something less valuable? Does that make a small human less valuable than a big human?

Also, teach people that animals are people. It's a nice opportunity. It's a simple idea and some people intuitively know that, but sometimes they need to hear it. Killing an animal is killing a person — an animal person, not a human person, but a person.

And then the point about intention. I think that's the crème de la crème of all this. Stop overthinking everything. Stop being so obsessed with the results of everything you do. Go into an inquiry: what's my intention, what's driving me, where am I really coming from? That's a beautiful class. Really accessible, and it's really leading people into Buddhist truths.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.note: Parents as objects of veneration — Eastern vs. Western perspectives
teaching.text: Something that kind of comes across from an Eastern cultural background — you'll see people of venerable respect like spiritual guides, and they throw in parents. For people of the East, that makes a lot of sense culturally. For people in America, in my view, that doesn't make as much sense. I don't ever really emphasize that personally, but do you — what do you think about that?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Kindness of parents; moving beyond blame
teaching.text:
Our parents could have had an abortion, which means we are not here. We are dead. Right? Getting killed in the womb. Every parent who did not do that is kind. They let us stay in their womb for nine months. They're legally allowed to terminate us if they wanted to. Many people do that, but they didn't do that. Having someone live in your body and putting your life on hold for nine months just to let you live, and then going through the painful ordeal of childbirth, is incredibly kind.

Many people who have bad childhoods — it's very easy to be ungrateful. A lot of Western people are a little bit weak-minded here. I'm not criticizing anyone. I'm just describing the situation. It's easy to blame our parents. But it's not our parents, it's our karma.

Our practice in seeing all living beings as a mother and developing gratitude for all living beings is contingent specifically on having gratitude for our own mother and father. It doesn't work totally if we haven't learned how to do it with our own parents, even with their incredible imperfection.

I've found sincere Dharma practitioners who really work this point in their own life, who had what a lot of people would classify as an absolutely awful childhood, have shifted their mind completely and radically with this stuff and just dropped it — dropped all the blame, dropped all the resentment, and have healed. And it's very inspiring to see.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: Since we're on the topic of mothers — how can we take this gratitude and deal with patience when it comes to them? I agree to have gratitude to her, but I can still get irritated by the way she talks or the way she asks questions or she is in denial, keeps asking the same questions the same way with different words. How can we use that gratitude? What's some tips? Because we definitely don't want to create more negative karma.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
I don't think there's a magic pill here. It's just trying to deepen the gratitude more and more. The more grateful we feel, the more love we feel, the more patient we become. It doesn't mean we need to talk to them all day. We have countless other mothers to care for and to benefit. But we try our best to give them extra special care.

When we love someone deeply, we're patient with them. So when we're getting annoyed, we've forgotten our love. In which case — okay, let's do some more meditation on that.

You could exchange self with that person for the nine months that they held us in their body. You can exchange self with her dealing with a husband who was probably not the easiest person ever. Just try to get in her mind — what's it like to be her from her point of view? You can also bring in other patience methods — someone's talking to me about things I'm not interested in. Well, how often have I done that and created that karma myself?

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: I was basically going to say the same thing — that what I like to do is just remember that I've been, and probably still am, that annoying mother to somebody else.

teaching.speaker: Mimi
teaching.text:
We also have to remember that our mothers aren't always going to be with us. With my own mom — she's a very, very strong woman, always really strong with me. And as she aged and developed age-related dementia, she's a different person. She's very soft and loving. I'm like, who? But I miss that hard mom.

She used to call me like five times a day — where are you? I'm working, why are you calling me? Now she doesn't call at all. Days will go by, weeks will go by. They change. And then when they pass away, you just — I'm going to miss her. I think we really have to value the time that we have, even if they're asking us annoying questions. My mom is constantly saying, Mimi, did you go buy Bounty? I'm like, Mom, you've got a whole closet full of Bounty. Then two minutes later — you need to go to the store. But I don't care how many times she asks me, because I'm going to miss her when she dies.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 366–370: Three effects of non-virtue; death meditation; the astrologer story
teaching.text:
Yeah, thanks, Mimi. It's a good point. We should meditate on the death of our parents too. Not just the gratitude of them, but their death. They will die, and they might die today, just like we will die and we might die today.

It's not Buddhist to blame anyone for our problems other than our negative karma.

As stated before, actions are called non-virtuous or unskillful because they lead to future suffering. There are three possible suffering effects of a particular non-virtuous action. The first, the fully ripened effect, is the future rebirth into which we are thrown by the ripening of the seed. The second result is called the effect similar to the cause. Finally, there is the environmental effect. Please check out Joyful Path of Good Fortune for the full breakdown.

As Shantideva pointed out, all the misery and frustration experienced in the various realms of samsara arise from our non-virtue. Fishermen may now be content to take the lives of fish, but how will they fare when tomorrow they themselves are born as fish? There's nothing permanent about our present human form. Feeling regret for our past non-virtue, we must find an antidote to this deadly poison immediately.

We have this huge snapping turtle in our pond at the temple right now. It's the mega apex predator in the pond. There's nothing that has any ability to withstand it. For me, it's a great image of the Lord of Death — because these fish have no choice. There's nothing they can do. It's faster, a better hunter, stronger, and has an unlimited appetite. So it just goes around all day eating all of them. That's me and the Lord of Death. He could be in the basement right now ready to come up and just tap me on the shoulder. I'm just like the fish in the pond — I can't bargain at that point.

In Tibet there once lived an astrologer famed for his outstanding ability to predict the future. One day he decided to find out when his own life would come to an end. Much to his surprise, he discovered that he was due to die that very day. While musing about whether he'd made a mistake, he leaned back, took his grooming kit from his pocket, and began cleaning out the wax from his ear with a needle-like piece of metal. All of a sudden, a burst of wind blew open the window he was leaning against. His arm was struck so sharply that the piece of metal was thrust through his eardrum and into his brain, killing him instantly. So who can be certain that death is not about to come?

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: So with all this death is uncertain — can we have a little purifying practice here before the summer? Because I can die until then. Can we have a purification practice? Like the full practice, the four powers? A day of prayers or something where we can do some more vigorous purification?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
I think it's a little late in the game to have something formally set up between today and summer. But there might be — we can think about it. If there's something that we could do in TTP next week that would be nice to do that's purifying, let's not talk about it right now as a group, but let's just think about it, or maybe in the break we can think about it. If there's something we can fit into the class, I'd be happy for us to do something that's purifying.

Maybe what we should have done is, as we went through this section, used something like the Vajrasattva practice instead of the normal prayers. That might have been the smarter thing to do. In retrospect, it's a little late to the game, but we could definitely do that next week.

And the Backyard Blowout Five is here, the fifth one, on the day after that. This will be my fifth. Very proud — me and Anne, I think, are the only ones who've been here five times. dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: Let's dedicate now. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications. Come back at 6:08 approximately.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
One thing we can ponder is: what's our relationship with impermanence? And how resistant are we to impermanence and change? Everything is changing all the time. We're in a river of change. And our mind is often trying to make things seem permanent out of some need for comfort, or some insecurity, or out of attachment. It's constantly trying to put a box on this river of change.

There's never a moment where things just stop and become still. But our mind is trying to quantify and reify and grasp all these different things, as they just flow right through our fingertips. So we can all explore this a little bit: do we have some resistance to change? And how does that affect us?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 371–374: Impermanence, death, purification urgency
teaching.text:
Geshe-la says here, page 94: In light of this uncertainty, we must purify our non-virtue immediately. There are many more circumstances that could bring about our death than those that tend to support our life. While all around us people are dying from accidents, war, and disease, how can we confidently expect to live out a normal lifespan? By thinking of the everyday examples we find in the news, we should meditate on the uncertainty of the time of death.

Think of our family, friends, relatives, and fellow countrymen. Who, among all of them, will still be around after 100 years have passed? Therefore, why do we commit so much wrong for the sake of beings who will disappear so soon?

Out of deep attachment, we have lied and stolen for the sake of our friends. With intense anger, we have directed much evil towards our enemies. The main cause for all the harm we have done is our ignorance of the law of actions and their effects. Not realizing that suffering will be the sole result of our actions, we ignorantly continue our non-virtuous behavior.

How difficult it is for us to understand that our life is racing towards the moment of death, and there is nothing we can do to prevent it. Second by second, our life force slips away. Unlike money, which will remain on deposit as long as we do not spend it, our lifespan is steadily dwindling. Now is the time to admit our non-virtue and practice all that is virtuous.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Death meditation and pure practice — Joyful Path of Good Fortune
teaching.text:
How is our meditation on death going? Has it improved over the last month, last year, the last five years? What's its role in our meditation arsenal?

From Joyful Path of Good Fortune, page 176: if we can develop equanimity with regard to the concerns of this life, we'll overcome many of our daily anxieties and frustrations. We'll find that we have more energy for our Dharma practice and that our practice becomes pure. Anyone who has developed equanimity with regard to worldly concerns has a high degree of spiritual attainments.

Therefore, in the beginning, our immediate aspiration should not be to gain the perfect results of Dharma practice. Rather, it should be to practice purely. If we can accomplish this aim, the results will come naturally in their own time. At the beginning of our training, if we're ambitious to experience results, this ambition itself will be an obstacle to our pure practice, because it will be mixed with attachment to worldly concerns. However, the ambition to practice purely is the well-balanced attitude of a steady practitioner.

We can check in our own practice: to what degree is it pure Dharma practice? Not done with worldly concerns? Meditating just to feel good is definitely a worldly concern. A lot of people's motivation is: I just want to feel good. This is just a worldly concern — just about seeking out some pleasure here and now. It's not about future lives. It's not motivated by benefiting others.

When we don't practice purely, we make a lot of mistakes. This happens in teaching also. If we're teaching for praise, we make strategic mistakes. We do a bunch of things to try to get praised, which is not always teaching Dharma correctly. Or we second-guess ourselves and get insecure because no one said it was a great class.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Anecdote: teaching purely and center flourishing
teaching.text:
I remember a friend of mine who's a Dharma teacher. When he first started teaching in his home country, he was a young monk, and he had a strong desire for his center to succeed. He was controlling how everything he was teaching would grow the center. But a lot of it was just not teaching purely — diluting the Dharma to try to make it more pop psychology, pop accessibility stuff. His center was an absolute wreck.

Then he got asked to go to another country, and he made a decision: I'm only going to teach pure Dharma. 100% don't care about external success. I'm going to teach what I was taught by my guru. And he said it was amazing, because his center flourished like wildfire. The intention was actually a bit contaminated, but the second he got the right intention — the aligned Dharma intention — all these blessings and inspirations started to flow.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Many people meditate on death just thinking 'I may die today,' but they haven't spent sufficient time thinking 'I will definitely die,' which is actually the first point. Traditionally there are three main points in meditation on death, each with three sub-points — nine points in total.

Point one: I will definitely die. Death will definitely come, nothing can prevent it. Our lifespan cannot be increased, and it decreases continuously. And death will come regardless of whether or not we've made the time to practice Dharma.

Point two: the time of death is uncertain. Our lifespan is not fixed. There are many more conditions conducive to death than to survival. The human body is very fragile — Nagarjuna says our human body is like a water bubble.

Point three: only Dharma can help us. At the time of death, our wealth cannot help us. Our friends and relatives cannot help us. Even our own body is of no use. The first Panchen Lama said: the body that we've cherished for so long cheats us at the time when we need it the most.

Without this last point, 'I may die today' doesn't have an outlet that is obviously virtuous. For the skillful Dharma practitioner, the thought 'I may die today' flows into 'therefore only Dharma can protect me.' It's like fuel. An ordinary person has no use for manure. For a farmer, it's a gift, because they have an outlet for it.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: On the point about practicing Dharma purely — I don't think I fully get it. Because in a sense, as long as I still have self-cherishing or delusions in general, there will be at some level concern for worldly concerns. So how do I know that I'm practicing purely?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Spectrum of pure practice; weaning off worldly concerns
teaching.text:
The worldly concerns are attachment to resources, pleasure, reputation, and praise. So it's checking: what's my motivation, my intention behind my Dharma practice?

There's a very broad spectrum. On one end: 100% self-cherishing and delusion, which is pretty hard to do and then do a Dharma practice. On the other end: we are a superior bodhisattva, realizing emptiness directly, meditating to benefit all living beings. In between, there are a ton of levels of purity.

So the question for each one of us is: how can we make it a bit more pure? When we sit down to meditate, to what degree am I meditating just for a quick feeling of pleasure right now? That's clearly worldly concern. How can I make that less impure? Can I also think about some people I love and make this meditation about benefiting them? That's less impure. Or we could think about our future lives, which doesn't count as a worldly concern because it's not about this life.

The idea is we just try to keep moving in that direction more and more. Eventually we gain realizations of renunciation, and then the meditations on great scope eliminate the worldly concerns completely.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 375–380: Logic, hell realms, correct reasoning
teaching.text:
Top of page 96. It is certain that if we do not begin to regret and purify the harm we've done, we'll be foolishly paving the way towards a future experience of hellish states. Yet some people firmly believe in the non-existence of such realms. They say that because they themselves cannot see such places, they must not exist at all. Such logic is ridiculous. We might as well say that because we cannot see what will happen tomorrow, the future is totally non-existent.

Furthermore, who can doubt the existence of experiences so horrific that people generally refer to them as 'living hells'? Living for months with excruciating pain, being trapped in paranoia or suicidal depression, having to face death by fire — these are only a few examples of easily recognizable hell-like sufferings experienced within our human realm.

Buddha Shakyamuni taught about the suffering realms not because he wished to frighten us, but because he wished to see us happy. When a mother explains to her young child the dangers of playing in a crowded street, she does so not because she wishes to scare her child. She teaches out of compassion.

In terms of our Dharma practice, a dread of lower states of rebirth should be cultivated now and not at the time of death. The fear that makes us cautious about our actions now is helpful, but the fear that arises at the time of death is not helpful at all. Before the fruits of our non-virtue ripen, we should purify our mind-stream. Once these fruits have already ripened, it is too late for even a Buddha to help. If we do not guard our actions, there is not much even a Buddha can do.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
In Buddhist practice, we have a very strict standard for something being logical. Most people in our modern world don't operate by these standards and only operate by probabilistic thinking. Probabilistic thinking is not logic — it's a guess. It has given up a desire for strict causality and settled for something that is reliable enough.

Syllogistic reasoning has three parts. The emptiness example from page 207: my body is empty of inherent existence because when I search for it with wisdom it disappears like a mirage. The property of the subject: when I search for my body with wisdom, it disappears. The forward pervasion: whatever disappears when we search for it with wisdom is necessarily empty of inherent existence. The reverse pervasion: if something were not empty of inherent existence, it would necessarily not disappear when we search for it with wisdom.

The easier example: there is fire in the house because there is smoke. Where there is smoke, there is fire. Where there is no smoke, there is no fire.

A lot of our thinking is just outsourced to experts of our choice — whatever outlet we like or whatever psychology book we read. But that is not logic. If we can strip our mind of these guesses and try to build up a worldview based on real logical truths, we will just deeply appreciate Buddha. It will help our faith a lot. The hell realms don't exist because I can't see them? That means anything I can't see doesn't exist. That's not good logic.

I think we can. So it'd be nice each day to target one of them — what would it be like to really purify my need for resources and security and outer security? What would it be like to purify that deep, almost unconscious need?

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Fran
practiceDiscussion.text: Because it feels like one of those things I'll never do with my ordinary mind. Never. I just won't. But Vajrasattva will absolutely knock that out of me.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: Yeah, I think so too. Some of these worldly concerns are so base and basic, so deep down, that it's a little bit hard to just use basic rationality to get at them. They're just so karmically embedded in our makeup that if we don't use something like purification as a big part of it, then it's a little hard to understand how to let go of them.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
Okay, I think that's good. Thank you, everyone. Back in action next week.

Let's dedicate. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make some personal dedications. And then in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

Don't forget about the NEDC, September 4th to the 7th — Teachings on the Liberating Prayer with Kadam Morton and Shakyamuni empowerment. Registration deadline is June 30th. It's Labor Day weekend, so make it your wild Labor Day plans if you can. It'd be nice for us to come as a nice sangha there.
